extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of aesthetics and moral philosophy (writers interested in moral-aesthetic effects)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentative criteria for composing and evaluating aesthetic/philosophical essays about taste, beauty, the sublime, and their moral utility. Emphasizes how aesthetic cultivation relates to virtue, social cohesion, and moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic communication unites society
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic communication alone unites society because it applies to what is common to all its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that pleasures of sense are individual and cannot be generalized, pleasures of knowledge can be generalized as a race, but beauty can be enjoyed both as individuals and as a race; thus aesthetic communication addresses what is common and unites people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty confers universal happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty alone confers happiness on all, and under its influence every being forgets that he is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts beauties' universal effect with goods appertaining to sense (which make one person happy) and absolute good (which can render a man happy only conditionally); suggests aesthetic experience can produce a universal, race-level happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste has no superior or absolute authority but governs appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste does not suffer any superior or absolute authority, and the sway of beauty is extended over appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste extends from the seat of reason's supremacy down to sensuous impulse; it maintains power on borders where legislation is taken from it, requiring particular desires to renounce egotism and adorn the mind with grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste demands moderation and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste demands of us moderation and dignity; it has a horror of everything sharp, hard and violent; it likes all that shapes itself with ease and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice this means aesthetic manners require restraint of brutish affections, graceful expression rather than coarse nudity, and that agreeable sensations must adorn the mind rather than merely satisfy senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste translates knowledge into common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste leads our knowledge from the mysteries of science into the open expanse of common sense, and changes a narrow scholasticism into the common property of the human race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest genius must make itself familiar to comprehension even of a child; strength must submit to Graces and the arbitrary must yield to love—taste makes intellectual achievements publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste veils physical necessity by offering an illusion of freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste throws a veil over physical necessity, dissimulating our degrading parentage with matter by a delightful illusion of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how taste elevates mercenary art and lifts the bondage of the bodily so that even slavish tools appear as free citizens in the aesthetic state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic appearance realizes equality
rubrics_metrics.description: In the realm of aesthetic appearance, the idea of equality is realized, which the political zealot would gladly see carried out socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In aesthetic state the most slavish tool is a free citizen with same rights as the noblest; the intellect shaping the mass must consult it concerning its destination—showing aesthetic equality across social distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic manners should stem from natural beauty not imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic circles where manners are not formed by the empty imitations of the foreign, but by the very beauty of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True aesthetic polity exists in select circles where man passes through complications with simplicity and innocence and without trenching on another's freedom or sacrificing dignity for grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste contributes to moral progress but is not a moral foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and pure feeling for the beautiful ought to exercise a salutary influence upon the moral life, but taste alone could never produce anything moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author insists morality's only foundation is morality itself; taste can favor morality in conduct but cannot replace the law of reason as the source of moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways taste can favor morality
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be two different ways of favoring morality: either strengthen the side of reason (the power of the good will) or break the force of temptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If we strengthen reason, moral will is less susceptible to temptation; if we break temptation's force (e.g., by aesthetic constraints), we make it easier for a feeble will inclined to good to act morally—both routes can favor moral conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutralizing resistance to duty favors morality
rubrics_metrics.description: All which neutralizes the resistance offered to the law of duty really favors morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the will itself isn't strengthened, removing or reducing obstacles to acting from duty (e.g., via taste) helps realization of moral actions; the text uses examples to show how diminished temptation enables morally good acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste governs the will by pleasure and so cannot itself ground morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste effectively governs the soul itself only by the attraction of pleasure; it is true of a nobler type because its principle is reason, but still as long as the will is determined by pleasure there is not yet morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because taste moves by feeling, actions motivated solely by taste—even if conforming with duty—are morally indifferent rather than moral; taste may precede conscience's judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated taste implants noble inclinations approximating virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivated taste implants in us nobler and gentler inclinations, which draw nearer to order, to harmony, and to perfection; and although these inclinations are not by themselves virtues, they have at least something in common with virtue; it is their object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those inclinations change appetites so that, even when appetite speaks, it must undergo control by the sense of the beautiful; thus taste disposes feelings toward duty and makes a mediocre will sufficient for virtuous practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic education secures legality when moral virtue is unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: If human nature cannot be expected always to act uniformly as pure reason, it is an obligation to satisfy at the very least the physical order by the object of our acts, even when we do not satisfy the exigencies of the moral order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because moral action is subject to chance and fragility, aesthetic education (like religion) provides bonds that assure legality and preserve the physical/social order when pure morality is uncertain—thus aesthetic rules have practical legal utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion and taste act as anchors for legality
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion and taste have the merit, similar in effect, although dissimilar in principle and in value, to take the place of virtue properly so called, and to assure legality where there is no possibility to hope for morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both supply salutary bonds to prevent crises when passion dominates; they serve as secondary supports that secure social order when pure moral will may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral education, not merely physical education, makes man entirely free
rubrics_metrics.description: The education that fits man for this [not suffering violence contrary to his will] is called moral education; the man fashioned by moral education, and he only, is entirely free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical education opposes force to force but has limits; moral education annihilates the idea of violence in relation to self, enabling resignation to necessity and true freedom of will independent of external forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime confirms moral independence by uniting pain and joy
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of the sublime is a mixed feeling... at once a painful state... and a joyous state... This union of two contrary sensations in one and the same feeling proves in a peremptory manner our moral independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the sublime brings simultaneous opposite responses, it shows that reason and sensuous nature relate differently to the object, revealing an autonomous principle independent of sensuous impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful harmonizes reason and sense; the sublime reveals their contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the presence of beauty, reason and sense are in harmony; in the presence of the sublime, on the contrary, reason and the sensuous are not in harmony, and it is precisely this contradiction which makes the charm of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beautiful teaches harmony and a sense of human liberty within nature; the sublime shows the separation of physical man and moral man, raising the moral to the infinite even while the physical feels its limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime objects either defy representation or overpower our vital forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime object may be considered in two lights: we either represent it to our comprehension and try in vain to make an image of it, or we refer it to our vital force and consider it as a power before which ours is nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both modes evoke painful feelings of limits yet attract us because by imagination or thought we can reach beyond the senses; the sublime thus points to capacities of will and reason that escape nature's empire.
